senses: Producing a large amount of torque.
A humanoid fictional character who has animal ears and/or tail(s).
ety: From Japanese 獣(けもの)耳(みみ) (kemonomimi), from 獣(けもの) (kemono, “animal”) + 耳(みみ) (mimi, “ear”).

senses: As much as a gut (abdomen) will hold.
examples: In every dark corner, fat black bin bags were bent double, throwing up gutfuls of old clothes.
Several gutfuls of alcoholic laughter-breath rolled around the room.
Stratonike laughed, great gutfuls of loud raucous laughter that carried across the crowd.

senses: Characterized by discontinuous or sporadic movement; jerky.
A highly venomous snake found in sub-Saharan Africa, Dispholidus typus.
ety: From Afrikaans boomslang, from Dutch boomslang, composed of boom (“tree”) + slang (“snake”).

senses: A Puerto Rican music genre associated with ballroom dancing.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish danza. Doublet of dance.
examples: Sunday at 2 p.m., a performance of classical Puerto Rican danza music by the Association for Puerto Rican Culture, featuring the pianist Alberto Bird and the singer Thelma Ithier-Sterling.

senses: A small dragon.
ety: From Middle English dragonet, from Middle French dragonet. By surface analysis, dragon + -et.

senses: That cannot be skipped.
A large, protruding, or swollen abdomen; a paunch.
A pinto horse with white-over-dark body markings.
examples: The dark overo cropouts often have wide blazes on the face and do not have the bald or apron faces that are associated with the overo color pattern.

senses: A motion in dancing, when one leg is a little bent and raised from the floor, and with the other a forward motion is made.
ety: Borrowed from French coupée, past participle of couper (“to cut”). Compare coupé, coopee.

senses: A non-commissioned officer, such as a sergeant (army) or petty officer (navy).
examples: Noncoms in uniform photograph you, full-face and profile; they take your fingerprints.

senses: Having multiple, simultaneous rhythms.
The soil region subject to the influence of plant roots and their associated microorganisms.
The act or result of scaling up.
A startup in the growth phase.
examples: I believe that we can visualize the typical lifecycle of startups and scaleups as a number of stages or game levels.

senses: Crawling around.
As if covered in moving things such as insects.
A color with bluish and purplish hues, somewhat light.
ety: Diminutive of Middle English perwinke, from Old English perfince, perwince (compare Middle High German berwinke), from Latin pervinca (compare French pervenche, Italian pervinca).

senses: A person who supplies or designs costumes.
The science of the properties, distribution, and effects of water on a planet's surface, in the soil and underlying rocks, and in the atmosphere.
The properties, distribution, and flows of water in a specific locale; the hydrological characteristics of a particular place or region.
examples: Operations studies are required to define appropriate hydrologies and facility operations schedules on which to base the Delta modeling.

senses: A rough cider, normally more alcoholic than usual, and typically produced through natural fermentation.
ety: From scrump + -y. Possibly related to scrumptious via roots referring to little amounts.

senses: The transcription of speech using symbols.
A form of shorthand using such symbols.
The art of constructing, or using, the phonograph.
An ornamental hairpin; hair ornament.
A manufacturer and vendor of drugs and medicines.
ety: From French droguiste, replacing earlier drugger. See drug.
examples: No druggist of the soul bestow'd on all / So catholicly a curing cordial.

senses: The edible fruit of these plants.
The wood of these plants.
Complete detachment or disunion.
To engage in fornication.
ety: First attested in 1552; borrowed from Latin fornicātus, perfect active participle of fornicor (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fornix (“arch, vault; brothel”). It was customary for courtesans of the era to wait for their customers out of the rain in arched passageways.

senses: Originating or occurring outside the liver.
examples: Extrahepatic duct abscess causes biliary colic, hepatic tenderness, vomiting, and intestinal disturbance.
Research is needed to define extrahepatic processes for uptake and distribution.

senses: A device that removes pits from fruit such as olives or cherries.
A person who makes or sells perfume.
One who perfumes something.
ety: From perfume (noun and verb) + -er, perhaps modelled on Middle French parfumeur.

senses: Inclined to swag; saggy.
A similar inflated bag used in performing stunts, or for lifting objects in firefighting, etc.
examples: As part of a scene in a movie, a stuntman falls from the top of a 95-foot-tall building into a large airbag directly below him on the ground, as shown in Figure 15-3.

senses: One who trashes something.
examples: He ends up falling in love with Jane Jerome, whose house he trashed, not knowing it was her, and she doesn't know he was one of the trashers.

senses: An anabolic steroid.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἀνα- (ana-, “up”) + βάλλω (bállō, “I throw”) + -ic.

senses: Having a sharp, pungent flavor.
A vehicle, usually a passenger car, with its suspension system modified so that it rides as low to level ground as possible without dragging.
Used to describe a dog known for its short legs (e.g. a dachshund, corgi, basset hound, etc.)
examples: The first lowriders were rounded models from the 1930s and 40s.

senses: A personal weapon, either a firearm (handgun type) or a cold weapon (such as a sword), carried on the hip in a belt, sheath, holster, etc., for rapid access.
Music written especially for Bollywood films.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi फ़िल्मी (filmī), ultimately from English film.

senses: Not codified, not part of the code of law, not stated as part of a systematic statement of principles.
A nestling; a young bird in the nest.
A red Italian alcoholic liqueur.
ety: From Middle French alkermès, probably from Spanish alquermes, from Arabic الْقِرْمِز (al-qirmiz), from Classical Persian کرمست (kirmist), from Middle Persian, from Sanskrit [Term?].
